content: With the consent of clients, mentor mothers collaborate with adherence counselors and social workers to monitor adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) and address barriers to successful treatment. This approach has demonstrated significant success, with attention to psychosocial issues resulting in high adherence rates and less than 1% of participants experiencing repeat teenage pregnancies. Disclosure of HIV status to parents, guardians, or partners is considered a critical component of adherence success. It fosters an environment of trust and support, and disclosure to a loved one is used as a measure of program success. Throughout the program, disclosure is treated as a life skill, with participants guided through the process using role-play discussions. These discussions help clients select appropriate individuals to disclose to, such as partners, family members, or friends, and determine whether they require assistance from a life coach, mentor mother, or trained counselor. Coaches involved in the program must have disclosed their own HIV status to a partner or family member to effectively support participants in this area. To scale up these efforts, collaboration with the Ministry of Health (MOH) includes capacity building for health workers to improve their skills in delivering services to adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV). Adolescents who have completed the program are engaged as peer support links for adolescent mothers attending antenatal or HIV treatment programs in the public health sector. Key factors contributing to the program's success include close collaboration with government entities, a team-based approach to adherence, peer-to-peer support strategies, the involvement of older women living with HIV as lay counselors or mentors, and the emphasis on HIV status disclosure as a core program component. Challenges facing the program include its limited geographic scope (operating in only three parishes and targeting ALHIV who are mothers) and limited funding, which threatens sustainability. Community-based service delivery is also employed to minimize risky behaviors and facilitate timely, low-cost referrals for prevention support when adolescents test negative for HIV. For those testing positive, adherence support involves home visits by health workers, lay counselors, and ALHIV peers, as well as the establishment of long-term relationships with health staff, partnerships with guardians, and the development of support groups for ALHIV. In South Africa, community-based adherence support (CBAS) workers provide regular adherence and psychosocial support for patients, conduct home visits to address household challenges affecting adherence, and assess family and household members in collaboration with patients. Issues are discussed at multidisciplinary clinic team meetings. A multicenter cohort study evaluating this intervention showed improved outcomes in patient retention, mortality, loss to follow-up, and viral suppression among adolescents receiving CBAS support. The Botswana-Baylor Children’s Clinical Centre of Excellence (COE) serves as a model for strengthening the continuum of care for children and adolescents with HIV. The COE provides a range of linked interventions, including a simplified disclosure process, adherence classes for caregivers, nutritional support, home visits, remedial education, adolescent support services, and structured transitioning to adult care. For pregnant adolescents, the program offers parenting skills training and encourages school reintegration or income-generating activities for those unable to return to school. The COE has achieved high retention rates and impacts over two-thirds of pediatric ART patients in Botswana. In Uzbekistan, services for ALHIV are integrated into existing systems through day-care centers (DCCs) for children and families affected by HIV. These centers provide psychosocial support at all stages of disclosure, create an enabling environment for transitioning adolescents into adult services, and strengthen connections between ALHIV across regions. Activities include psychological counseling, self-support groups, educational materials, and online platforms to enhance peer relationships. However, challenges include a lack of enabling environments for ALHIV, delayed entry into care due to nondisclosure, and insufficient support systems post-diagnosis. The Zvandiri program in Zimbabwe, led by adolescents with HIV, integrates community-based treatment, care, support, and prevention services with government and private-sector clinical care. Community Adolescent Treatment Supporters (CATS) provide adherence monitoring, support in clinics and homes, and assistance in identifying adolescents at risk of treatment failure. The program also includes sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, linking young people to care for STIs, family planning, and prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). Zvandiri has been recognized as a best practice model for sustainable HIV care and prevention services for children and adolescents. In South Africa, evaluations of lay counselor adherence support revealed gaps in client-centered counseling approaches. Regular supervision focusing on micro-counseling skills and avoiding inappropriate strategies is recommended to improve adherence outcomes.
